title: SLIs, SLOs, Error Budgets
description: Learn to define meaningful SLIs, set achievable SLOs, and use error budgets to make data-driven decisions about reliability vs velocity, following Google's SRE approach.

segments.text: Most teams monitor everything but measure nothing meaningful. CPU at seventy percent? Is that good or bad? SLIs, SLOs, and error budgets give you a framework to answer the only question that matters: are your users happy? Google's SRE team built this framework after realizing uptime alone was a terrible metric.

An SLI — Service Level Indicator — is a quantitative measure of service health. The key insight: measure at the user boundary, not inside your infrastructure. Good SLIs: request latency at p99, error rate as a percentage of total requests, availability as successful requests divided by total requests.

Bad SLIs kill your reliability program. Average latency hides outliers — your p50 could be fifty milliseconds while p99 is five seconds. CPU utilization measures infrastructure, not user experience. QPS measures load, not quality. Always choose SLIs that correlate with user-perceived quality.

An SLO — Service Level Objective — is a target for your SLI. Ninety-nine point nine percent availability sounds great until you do the math. That's eight hours and forty-five minutes of allowed downtime per year. Four nines — ninety-nine point ninety-nine percent — gives you only fifty-two minutes. Each additional nine costs exponentially more to achieve.

Your VP wants five nines — ninety-nine point nine nine nine percent. That's five minutes and fifteen seconds of downtime per year. A single deploy rollback takes longer than that. Is five nines realistic for your service?
segments.thought_prompt: What would it take to achieve five nines? Is it worth the engineering investment?

segments.text: The error budget is the inverse of your SLO. If your SLO is ninety-nine point nine percent, your error budget is zero point one percent — you're allowed to fail zero point one percent of requests. This month, if you've used only thirty percent of your error budget, ship aggressively. If you've used ninety percent, slow down and focus on reliability.

Burn rate alerts tell you how fast you're consuming your error budget. A burn rate of one means you'll exhaust the budget exactly at month's end. A burn rate of ten means you'll exhaust it in three days. Google recommends alerting at burn rates of fourteen for a one-hour window and six for a six-hour window. This catches both fast burns and slow bleeds.

The error budget policy is where SRE meets management. When the error budget is exhausted: freeze feature deployments, redirect engineering effort to reliability work, require post-mortems for every incident. When budget is healthy: ship fast, take risks, experiment. This creates a self-regulating system.

Google's SRE handbook defines the contract between SRE and product teams. Product sets the SLO based on user needs, SRE enforces it. If a team repeatedly exhausts their error budget, SRE can hand the pager back to the development team. This creates real accountability — you build it, you run it.
You're setting SLOs for a payment processing system. It handles ten million transactions per day. What SLIs would you choose, what SLO targets, and what should the error budget policy include?
segments.thought_prompt: Design SLIs, SLOs, and error budget policy for a payment system processing 10M transactions/day.

segments.text: SLIs measure what users care about — latency, errors, availability. SLOs set targets that balance reliability with development velocity. Error budgets turn reliability into a measurable, manageable resource. The Staff-level insight: SLOs are not about perfection. They're about making rational trade-offs between shipping features and maintaining reliability.
